title: Judicial Review and Basic Structure

cards.b:
Judicial review is the power of courts to test laws and executive acts against the Constitution and strike down those that violate it. The basic structure doctrine goes further: even a constitutional amendment cannot destroy the Constitution's core features.

Together they decide who has the last word: Parliament or the Supreme Court. This is among the most important themes in Paper I, linked to nearly every other topic, from rights to federalism.

The idea has US roots in Marbury v. Madison (1803). In India, the Constitution gives textual support through Article 13 (laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void), Article 32 and 226 (writs), Articles 131-136 (jurisdiction) and Articles 124 onwards (the judiciary).

Examiners ask: What is the basic structure? How did the doctrine evolve? Is it undemocratic? How has the Court used it? Prepare a case timeline and a few current examples.

The idea of implied limits came from German jurist Dietrich Conrad, whose 1965 lecture at Banaras Hindu University was cited by Justice Mudholkar in his Sajjan Singh dissent. Nani Palkhivala argued the case for the petitioners in Kesavananda.

Swami Kesavananda challenged Kerala's land reform laws, which were placed in the Ninth Schedule. A 13-judge bench, the largest in the Court's history, heard it for 68 days. The 7:6 verdict held:

  • Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, under Article 368.
  • But it cannot change the basic structure or framework of the Constitution.
  • Different judges listed different features: Sikri (supremacy, republican and democratic form, secular character, separation of powers, federalism); Shelat and Grover added the mandate to build a welfare state and the unity and integrity of the nation; Hegde and Mukherjea added the sovereignty of India and the essential features of individual freedoms; Khanna's concurrence was decisive.
  • Article 31C was upheld in part: laws for Article 39(b)-(c) are protected but still open to review.

A day later, on 26 April 1973, A.N. Ray became Chief Justice, superseding three senior judges (Shelat, Hegde, Grover). It was widely seen as a response to the verdict.

cards.h: After Kesavananda: the Emergency and recovery
cards.b:
• Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975): the Court struck down the 39th Amendment's clause removing the PM's election from judicial scrutiny, citing free and fair elections and rule of law as basic features.
  • ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976): during the Emergency, a 4:1 majority said no habeas corpus remedy was available. Justice H.R. Khanna's lone dissent became famous. The ruling was overruled by Puttaswamy (2017).
  • 42nd Amendment (1976): tried to put amendments beyond review.
  • Minerva Mills (1980): struck down the clauses; limited amending power and the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are basic.
  • Waman Rao (1980): Ninth Schedule laws before 24 April 1973 are protected.
  • I.R. Coelho (2007): laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after that date can be reviewed on rights and basic structure.

cards.h: The accepted list of basic features
cards.b:
The Court has never given an exhaustive list. Features recognised in cases include:

  • Supremacy of the Constitution, and the rule of law.
  • Sovereign, democratic, republican structure; parliamentary democracy.
  • Secularism (Bommai, 1994) and federalism.
  • Separation of powers, independence of the judiciary and judicial review (L. Chandra Kumar, 1997).
  • Free and fair elections (Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain, 1975).
  • Fundamental Rights' essence and the balance with Part IV (Minerva Mills).
  • Unity and integrity of the nation; equality and the "golden triangle" of Articles 14, 19 and 21.
  • Welfare state, social justice and the principle of reasonableness.

Note: the doctrine tests constitutional amendments. Ordinary laws are tested against specific provisions, as the Court clarified in State of A.P. v. McDowell (1996).

Other countries have followed the idea, including Bangladesh (Anwar Hossain Chowdhury, 1989).

cards.h: Judicial review in action and the judges' appointments
cards.b:
• Writs under Article 32/226: habeas corpus, mandamus, certiorari, prohibition, quo warranto.
  • PIL: relaxed locus standi since the late 1970s. Hussainara Khatoon (1979) on undertrial prisoners and Vishaka (1997) on sexual harassment, where the Court made guidelines in the absence of a law.
  • Appointments: S.P. Gupta (First Judges Case, 1981) gave the executive primacy; the Second Judges Case (1993) established the collegium and the CJI's primacy; the Third (1998, Presidential reference) set it as the CJI and four senior-most judges.
  • 99th Amendment and NJAC: struck down in the Fourth Judges Case on 16 October 2015 (4:1, Justice Chelameswar dissenting) as breaching independence of the judiciary, a basic feature.
  • Article 142 allows orders for "complete justice". It has been used for broad directions, and critics say it can be overstretched.

cards.h: What the courts review besides statutes
cards.b:
• Administrative action: tests of legality, reasonableness (the Wednesbury test), proportionality and fair procedure (natural justice). Maneka Gandhi made fairness part of Article 14 and 21.
  • Ordinances: in D.C. Wadhwa (1987), repeated re-promulgation of ordinances was held a fraud on the Constitution. Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) confirmed that the satisfaction of the President or Governor is reviewable.
  • Emergency and President's Rule: reviewable after Bommai (1994); the 38th and 44th Amendments' effect on Article 352 and 356.
  • Mercy and pardon: reviewable on limited grounds (Epuru Sudhakar, 2006).
  • Tribunals: in L. Chandra Kumar (1997) the Court held that High Court and Supreme Court review over tribunals cannot be excluded. The Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 was challenged on independence grounds.
  • Parliamentary proceedings: courts avoid interfering in internal matters (Article 122), but Speakers' decisions on defection are reviewable (Kihoto Hollohan, 1992).

Rule of thumb: courts judge legality, not wisdom. Yet that line moves as new rights are recognised.

The case for: the doctrine protects minorities from a transient majority and stopped the Emergency-era attempts to place the executive beyond law. H.R. Khanna's dissent in ADM Jabalpur and his role in Kesavananda are held up as moral anchors.

The case against:

  • Alexander Bickel called this the counter-majoritarian difficulty in The Least Dangerous Branch (1962): unelected judges overturning elected representatives.
  • The basic structure is judge-defined and vague, so the Court becomes the final author of the Constitution.
  • Collegium opacity: judges appoint judges, with little transparency.
  • Judicial overreach: the Court has set policy on pollution, vehicles and cricket administration.

S.P. Sathe (Judicial Activism in India, 2002) distinguished legitimate activism from overreach; Upendra Baxi and Rajeev Dhavan wrote critically on the Court's role. Balanced conclusion: the doctrine is an essential check, but the Court must use restraint and open its own appointment process.

cards.h: The Court and the political branches, 2023-2026
cards.b:
• Article 370 (11 December 2023): the Court upheld the revocation of J&K's special status, adopting a deferential approach.
  • Electoral bonds (15 February 2024): struck down on voters' right to information.
  • Tamil Nadu v. Governor (8 April 2025): used Article 142 to set time limits and "deemed assent"; critics, including the then Vice-President, questioned the use of Article 142. In November 2025, a five-judge bench answering the Presidential reference said courts cannot fix such deadlines.
  • Waqf Act (15 September 2025): partial stay, with the Court saying it will be slow to stay statutes.
  • SIR of electoral rolls: upheld in May 2026 as within the Election Commission's powers.
  • Delimitation and ONOE: arguments about whether changes affect the federal structure or electoral equality, which could return to the basic-structure debate if they pass.
  • Chief Justice Surya Kant (from 24 November 2025) leads the Court until February 2027.

"Explain the doctrine of basic structure. How has it protected the Constitution?"
"Judicial review versus parliamentary sovereignty: which should prevail in India?"
"Judicial activism has become judicial overreach." Examine.
"Evaluate the collegium system and the NJAC verdict."

Structure: define judicial review and Article 13; evolution (Shankari Prasad to Kesavananda); features; post-1973 cases (Raj Narain, Minerva Mills, Coelho); appointments (three judges cases, NJAC); critique (Bickel, Sathe); current examples (electoral bonds, Governors' case, Waqf); close with a case for restraint plus transparency.
